STRIDES

Self-supervised Temporal Re-Identification of DEndritic Spines

Sophie L. Hauser, Ananya Sachdev, Alessio Attardo, Andreas M. Kist

Spine re-identification across sessions

  • Spine at Tt
  • Spine transfer
  • Re-identified position
  • Annotation at Tt+1
  • Outside tolerance

Example stack (mouse 79, Thy1-eGFP, region A4), maximum-intensity projections, contrast adjusted for display. The annotated spines at session Tt (left) are re-identified at Tt+1 (right). A match counts as within tolerance when it lies within 0.7 µm laterally and 1.5 µm axially of the annotation (voxel size 0.107 × 0.107 × 0.5 µm). Hover or tap a spine for its track ID and error.

Abstract

Dendritic spines are highly dynamic structures whose changes over time reflect structural plasticity in the brain. Manually re-identifying individual spines in longitudinal microscopy images, however, is time-consuming and error-prone. We present STRIDES, a framework for Self-supervised Temporal Re-Identification of DEndritic Spines. STRIDES first estimates each spine's coarse location in the next image stack using feature matching and axial alignment. It then refines this location using embeddings from a foundation model fine-tuned with self-supervised triplet learning and an optimization that preserves the arrangement of neighboring spines. Human annotations are only needed to tune the optimization weights, minimizing the influence of annotation errors. On two longitudinal datasets, STRIDES consistently outperformed the recent tracking method SynapFlow, correctly matching up to 77.5% of spines within a strict distance tolerance and 97.5% with nearest-neighbor assignment.

How STRIDES works

STRIDES needs only the spine positions at the first time point. For every pair of sessions it predicts where each spine is in the next stack, and the predictions become the query points of the step after.

1Initial estimate in x, y

SuperPoint and LightGlue match features between the maximum-intensity projections of both stacks. Each spine is transferred to the next session with the interpolated displacement of its nearest matched features, so it keeps its position relative to them.

2Initial estimate in z

Every slice of one stack is matched against every slice of the other. The diagonal with the highest summed match score gives the z-offset Δz between the stacks, which places each spine in depth.

3Refinement

A DINOv3-based encoder embeds a small crop around each spine at Tt, and a crop around every voxel of a region of interest centred on the initial estimate p0. Their cosine similarity gives one 3D similarity map per spine.

All spines are then optimized together: each is pulled toward the soft centre of mass of its similarity map, while the pairwise distances of the point set are preserved and the result stays close to the initial estimate.

Self-supervised training

The encoder is fine-tuned without labels. A crop around a random foreground voxel (anchor) and a copy of the same region rotated in 3D (positive; any in-plane angle, up to ±3° tilt) should map to the same embedding, while crops of other regions in the batch (negatives) are pushed away with a semi-hard triplet loss. Noise, blur and brightness offsets are applied to every crop. We trained on the public DeepD3 dataset.

Code and GUI

The repository contains the inference pipeline, a graphical user interface and the training code. Input is a 4D TIFF with axes (T, Z, Y, X); the spines of the first time point are clicked in the interface or loaded from a CSV.

Installation

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate strides
git clone https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov3.git
Model weights. Download the fine-tuned STRIDES encoder and save it as checkpoints/strides_embedder.pth in the repository: strides_embedder.pth (link follows). Access to the pretrained DINOv3 backbone is described in the DINOv3 repository.

Graphical user interface

  1. Open stack. Two consecutive time points are shown side by side; the slider scrolls through the slices of both.
  2. Query points. Click spines in the left stack, or load a CSV with POSITION_X, POSITION_Y, POSITION_Z.
  3. Run inference. The re-identified spines appear in the right stack, which is shifted by the z-offset found.
  1. Correct. Drag a point, Shift-click to place it on another slice, right-click to remove it, Ctrl+Z to undo.
  2. Save & next timepoint. The tracks are written to a CSV and the re-identified spines become the next query points.
cd inference
python gui.py

Developed with Python 3.10 and PyTorch 2.9.1 (CUDA 12.6). The code is released under Apache-2.0. The DINOv3 backbone and checkpoints fine-tuned from it are covered by the DINOv3 License; the SuperPoint weights used through LightGlue have their own license.
